column2: To him whose feet are reddened by the crest-jewels of gods and asuras, the beloved one who gave half his body to his own beloved, salutations again and again.
This hymn to Mahesha has been declared, destroying all sins, granting Shiva's presence, O brahmin, and illuminating the tantra of serpents.
This very great tantra reveals all the gods and is joined with the rites and means for fulfilling the world's desires.
The mantras stated in general in this tantra, O brahmin, are to be known as granting success for the benefit of the world;
but the Vaishnava mantras especially are the best of all; they alone should be practised to gain the fruit of the four aims of life.
The mantras of Rama and of Krishna with their limbs, the mantras of the lord of the rasa, and the Shakta, Saura, Ganapatya and Shaiva mantras are declared auspicious.

Among them, for the revelation of one's own Self one should worship those that give the fruit of liberation. All this I have told you, O sage, as you asked — the worship of the deities with devotion; what more do you wish to hear?
Dividing it into eighteen, he sets it forth in the world of men; even today in the world of the gods it extends to a hundred crores,
and its essence is described in four lakhs: the Brahma, Padma, Vishnu and Vayu Puranas,
the Bhagavata, the Naradiya and the Markandeya are named; the Agni, the Bhavishya, the Brahmavaivarta and the Linga,
the Varaha, the Skanda, the Vamana, the one called Kurma, the Matsya, the Garuda and likewise the one called Brahmanda — thrice six.
I will tell you in brief the single thread of their stories, with the names of speaker and hearer; listen attentively.
First among them is the Brahma Purana, declared for the welfare of all worlds by the great-souled Vyasa, knower of the Veda.
It is foremost of all the Puranas, granting dharma, pleasure, wealth and liberation, rich in many stories and histories, and is said to have ten thousand verses.
In it are told the origin of the gods and asuras, and of the Prajapatis beginning with Daksha, O lord of sages;
then the holy account of the lineage of the Sun, lord of the world and supreme Self, which destroys great sins;
where is told the incarnation of the glorious Ramachandra, whose form is supreme bliss, who incarnated in four forms;
then where the account of the lunar dynasty is described, and the sin-destroying story of Krishna, lord of the world;
where the description of all the continents and all the regions, and of the netherworlds and heavens, is seen;
the account of the hells, the story of the hymn to the Sun, and the birth and marriage of Parvati are told;
then the story of Daksha and the description of the sacred field of Ekamra. This is declared the first part of this Purana, O Narada.
In its latter part the description of Purushottama is given at length, with the procedure of pilgrimage;
here too the story of Krishna is told at length, the description of Yama's world and the procedure of shraddha for the ancestors;
where the dharmas of the classes and stages of life are declared at length, the story of Vishnu's dharma and the ages, and the description of dissolution;
the account of the yogas and the description of the Sankhyas, the exposition of the doctrine of Brahman, and the praise of the Purana.
This Brahma Purana, consisting of two parts, has been described; it destroys all sins and grants all happiness.
It is the dialogue of Suta and Shaunaka, granting enjoyment and liberation. Whoever writes out this Purana and on the full moon of Vaishakha, with gold
and with a water-cow, gives it with devotion to a brahmin, a reciter of Puranas, honouring him with clothes, food and ornaments,
dwells in Brahma's world as long as the moon, sun and stars endure. Whoever reads or hears the index of the Brahma Purana, O brahmin,
also gains the fruit of hearing and reciting the whole Purana. Whoever, with senses controlled, hears the whole Brahma Purana,
eating only sacrificial food and keeping discipline, attains Brahma's state. What need of more words? Whatever a man desires, he obtains all of it, child, by reciting this Purana.
This is the fifth, the latter section, granting all merit. The best of men who hears the Padma Purana with its five sections
attains Vishnu's abode after enjoying the pleasures he desires here. This Purana called Padma has fifty-five thousand verses.
Whoever has this Purana written out and, on the full moon of Jyeshtha, gives it with a golden lotus, with due honour, to one who knows the Puranas, O giver of honour,
goes to Vishnu's abode, saluted by all the gods. Whoever reads or hears this index of the Padma
also gains the fruit born of hearing the Padma Purana.
He removed the earth's burden by slaying others and the like; the story of Ashtavakra — this is declared the fifth part.
The conduct of the Kali age is told, the fourfold dissolution, and the teaching on the knowledge of Brahman given to Khandikya
by Keshidhvaja — this is declared the sixth part. After this, Suta, asked respectfully by Shaunaka and the others,
related the Vishnudharmottara: many holy stories of dharma, vows, disciplines and restraints,
the science of dharma, the science of polity, Vedanta and astronomy, accounts of lineages as occasion arose, hymns and mantras,
and various branches of learning beneficial to all people. This Vishnu Purana is the compendium of the meaning of all scriptures,
the account of the Varaha kalpa, told here by Vyasa. The man who reads it with devotion and the one who hears it with reverence
both go to Vishnu's world after enjoying pleasures. Whoever writes it out and gives it on the full moon of Ashadha with a ghee-cow
to a devotee of Vishnu who knows the meaning of the Puranas, O brahmin, goes to Vishnu's abode in a celestial car shining like the sun.
And whoever recites or hears the index of the Vishnu Purana, O brahmin, gains the fruit of the Purana.
Then the story of Vritra, and the holy birth of the Maruts — this is declared by Vyasa the sixth book, on nourishment (poshana).
The holy story of Prahlada and the exposition of the classes and stages of life — this is told as the seventh, child, on the account of latent impressions and actions.
The story of the release of the king of elephants in the exposition of the manvantaras, the churning of the ocean, the glory and binding of Bali,
and the story of the Fish incarnation — this is declared the eighth. The account of the solar dynasty and the exposition of the lunar dynasty
in the account of lineages — this is declared the ninth, O wise one. Krishna's childhood, boyhood and stay in Vraja,
his adolescence and stay in Mathura, his youth and stay in Dvaraka, and the removal of the earth's burden — this, on restraint (nirodha), is known as the tenth.
The dialogue of Vasudeva with Narada is told, of Yadu with Dattatreya, and of Shri Krishna with Uddhava,
and the mutual destruction of the Yadavas — this, on liberation, is known as the eleventh. The prediction of the coming Kali age, the liberation of King Parikshit,
the arrangement of the branches of the Veda, the austerity of Markandeya, the glory of the Sun, and then the Satvata,
and the statement of the numbers of the Puranas — this, on the refuge, is the twelfth. Thus the Shrimad Bhagavata has been told to you, child;
it is declared to grant devotion, enjoyment and liberation to the speaker, the hearer, the instructor, the approver and the helper.
On the full moon of Proshthapada it should be given with a golden lion, lovingly, to a brahmin devotee of the Lord,
honouring him with clothes, gold and the like, by one who desires devotion to the Lord. Whoever has this index recited or hears it obtains the excellent fruit born of hearing the Purana.
The applications, the armour, the thousand names and the hymns of Ganesha, the Sun, Vishnu, Shiva and Shakti in order,
told by the sage Sanatkumara to Narada in the third part; and the characteristics of a Purana, its extent and the gift,
stated separately with the time of giving; and in all the months beginning with Chaitra, separately for each lunar day,
the vows of the first and other lunar days, destroying all sins, told by the sage Sanatana to Narada in the fourth part.
This is declared the first part, called the Brihadakhyana. In its latter part is the question about the Ekadashi vow,
and the dialogue of Mandhatri with Vasishtha is related; the holy story of Rukmangada and the origin and deeds of Mohini,
the curse of the Vasus on Mohini and then her deliverance; the most holy story of the Ganga and the account of the pilgrimage to Gaya,
the incomparable greatness of Kashi, the description of Purushottama, the procedure of pilgrimage to that field, with many stories,
then the greatness of Prayaga, then of Kurukshetra, the story of Haridvara and the story of Kamoda,
the greatness of the tirtha of Badari and of Kamakhya, the greatness of Prabhasa, then the story of Pushkara,
then the story of Gautama, then the Vedapada hymn, the greatness of the field of Gokarna and the story of Lakshmana,
the account of the greatness of the Setu, the description of the tirthas of the Narmada, the greatness of Avanti and then of Mathura,
the glory of Vrindavana, the going of the beast to Brahma's presence, and then the story of Mohini — thus is the Naradiya.
The man who hears it with devotion or has it recited with concentration goes to Brahma's abode; there is no need to doubt this.
Whoever gives it on the full moon of Ishu with seven cows to an excellent brahmin gains liberation itself.
And whoever recites this index of the Naradiya, or hears it with a single mind, also attains the path to heaven.
The account of the war of gods and asuras, the exposition of Ayurveda, the treatment of elephants and others and their pacification,
the treatment of cows, men and others, then various worships, various pacificatory rites, then the science of metre,
then poetics, then lexicons of single letters and the like, the teaching of perfected words, and a dictionary arranged in groups beginning with creation,
the characteristics of the dissolutions, the exposition of the body, the description of the hells, then the science of yoga,
then the knowledge of Brahman, and then the fruit of hearing the Purana — this, O brahmin, is declared to be the Agni Purana.
Whoever writes it out and gives it, with a golden pen and with a sesame-cow, on the full moon of Margashirsha according to rule,
to one who knows the meaning of the Puranas, is honoured in the world of heaven. This index of the Agni Purana has been told to you; it grants liberation
to men who hear and read it, here and hereafter.
Among these five, in the first the greatness of Brahma predominates; in dharma, pleasure and liberation, that of Vishnu and of Shiva;
in the second and third, and in the solar one, the four aims; the last, called Pratisarga, is declared to contain all stories.
The book with the Bhavishya has been set out by the wise Vyasa; the Purana is declared to have fourteen thousand verses.
The Bhavishya is where the equality of all the gods is declared, with gradation of qualities; 'Brahman is the same,' says scripture.
The learned one free from envy who writes it out and gives it on the full moon of Pausha, with a jaggery-cow, gold, clothes, garlands and ornaments,
having duly worshipped the reciter and the book with perfumes and the like, with foods and eatables, and performed the waving of lights,
and whoever, having conquered his senses, fasting and concentrated, or eating only sacrificial food once, recites or hears it,
is freed from terrible sins and goes to Brahma's state. And whoever reads or hears this index of the Bhavishya
obtains enjoyment and liberation.
Then Hari's going to Mathura with Akrura; after the slaying of Kamsa and the others, Krishna's brahminical sacraments,
then the wondrous acquisition of learning from Sandipani of Kashi, the slaying of the Yavana, then Hari's going to Dvaraka,
and the wondrous slaying of Naraka and others by Krishna there. This Krishna section, O brahmin, cuts off men's worldly existence
when read, heard, meditated on, worshipped and saluted. Such is this very unworldly Brahmavaivarta Purana.
Told by Vyasa and arising from the beginning, one who reads or hears it is freed from the terrible ocean of worldly existence through the quelling of ignorance by knowledge.
Whoever writes this out and gives it on the full moon of Magha with a cow attains Brahma's world, freed from the bonds of ignorance.
And whoever reads or hears the index also obtains the fruit he desires by Krishna's grace.
Vajreshvari, the great knowledge, then the greatness of the Gayatri, the greatness of Tryambaka and of hearing the Purana.
Thus I have told you the latter part of the Linga, composed by Vyasa, which indicates the greatness of Rudra.
Whoever writes out this Purana and gives it with a sesame-cow on the full moon of Phalguna with devotion to a brahmin
gains union with Shiva, free from old age and death. The man who reads or hears the sin-removing Linga Purana
enjoys pleasures in this world and at the end goes to Shiva's city. Whoever reads this index of the Linga, and whoever hears it,
both become devotees of Shiva, enjoying both worlds, by the grace of Girija's husband; there is no doubt.
The story of Mahatapas, then the origin of Gauri, of Vinayaka, of the Nagas, of Senani and of the Adityas,
of the Ganas, of the Goddess, of the lord of wealth and of the bull; the story of Satyatapas with the stories of vows,
then the Agastya Gita and the Rudra Gita are declared, and the greatness of the destruction of Mahishasura, born of the three Shaktis,
then the chapter on festivals, the story of Shveta and the gift of cows — such events I have shown in the first part.
Then in the Bhagavaddharmaka, the stories of vows and tirthas, the bodily expiation for the thirty-two offences,
and the greatness of all the tirthas declared separately, especially of Mathura, then the procedure of shraddha and the like,
the description of Yama's world in connection with the sage's son, the ripening of karmas and the exposition of the vows of Vishnu,
and the sin-destroying greatness of Gokarna is declared. Thus the first part of this Purana has been set out.
In the latter part, in the dialogue of Pulastya and the king of the Kurus, the greatness of all the tirthas is given separately at length,
all the dharmas are told, and the holy Pushkara section. Thus the sin-destroying Varaha has been told to you,
increasing devotion to the Lord in those who read and hear it. Making a golden Garuda with a sesame-cow,
whoever writes this out and gives it on the full moon of Chaitra to a brahmin with devotion gains Vishnu's abode, praised by the hosts of gods and sages.
And whoever hears or reads this index also gains devotion to Vishnu, which cuts off worldly existence.
Mundira and the others, the three Arkas, the one called Sati's wedding, Rudrashirsha, Yagesha, Valakhilya and Garuda,
Lakshmi's curse, the twenty-seven, Soma's temple, Ambabaddha, the one called Panduka, Agneya and Brahmakundaka,
Gomukha, the one called Lohayashti, Ajapaleshvari, Shanaishchara, Rajavapi, Ramesha and Lakshmaneshvara,
the one called Kushesha and the one called Lavesha, the most excellent of lingas, the account of the sixty-eight, the three births of Damayanti,
then Revati here, the origin of the Bhaktika tirtha, Kshemankari and Kedara, Shuklatirtha and Mukharaka,
the story of Satyasandheshvara and the tale of Karnotpala, Ateshvara, Yajnavalkya, the Gauri and the Ganesha [tirthas],
then the story of Vastupada, the tale of Ajagriha, Saubhagyandhu, Shulesha and the tale of Dharmaraja,
the story of Mishtanneshvara, then the three Ganapatyas, the story of Jabali, then the tale of Makaresha,
the story of Kaleshvari and Andhaka, Kunda and Apyarasa, Pushyaditya, Rauhitashva and the account of the origin of the Nagaras,
the story of Bhargava, then that of Vishvamitra, the Sarasvata, the Paippalada, Kamsarisha and Paindaka,
the story of Brahma's sacrifice with the story of Savitri, Raivata, the one called Bhartriyajna, and the view of the chief tirthas,
Kaurava, the one called Hatakesha, Prabhasa — the three fields; Pushkara, Naimisha and Dharmaranya are remembered as the three forests;
Varanasi, the one called Dvaraka and the one called Avanti are the three cities; Vrindavana, the one called Khandava and the one called Advaika are the three groves;
Kalpa, Shala and Nandigrama are the three unsurpassed villages; the ones called Asi, Shukla and Pitri are declared the three tirthas;
Shri, Arbuda and Raivata are the three excellent mountains; the three rivers are the Ganga, the Narmada and the Sarasvati.
Each of these is declared to give the fruit of three and a half crores. Kushika, Shankhatirtha, Amaraka and Balamandana —
these four are declared to give the fruit of the field of Hatakesha. Sambaditya, the Shraddhakalpa, the Yaudhishthira, then Andhaka,
Jalashayi, the four months, the vow of Ashunyashayana, Mankanesha, Shivaratri and the gift of the Tulapurusha,
the gift of the earth, Vanakesha, Kapalamochaneshvara, Papapinda, Masalinga, and the account of the measures of the ages,
the one called Nimvesha-Shakambhari, the account of the eleven Rudras, the account of the greatness of giving, and the account of the twelve Adityas —
such is the Nagara section. Now the one called Prabhasa is told, where Someshvara, Vishvesha and the great holy place of the Sun are,
and the story of Siddheshvara and others is declared separately here; Agnitirtha, Kapardi and Kedaresha, who grants the goal,
Bhima, Bhairava, Chandisha, Bhaskara, Indu and Kujeshvara, Budha, Ijya, Bhrigu, Saura, Agu, Shikhi and Isha — forms of Hara;
five other Rudras beginning with Siddheshvara are established there; Vararoha, Aja, Pala, Mangala and Laliteshvari,
Lakshmisha, Vadavesha, Urvisha and Kameshvara, those called Gaurisha and Varunesha, Durvasesha and Ganeshvara,
Kumaresha, Chandakalpa and the one called Shakulishvara; then the good stories of Kotisha, Balabrahma and others are declared,
then the stories of Narakesha, Samvartesha and Nidhishvara, then of Balabhadreshvara, of the Ganga and of Ganapa,
the good story of the river called Jambavati and of Pandukupa, and the stories of Shatamedha, Lakshamedha and Kotimedha,
the grand story of Durvasarka, Ghatasthana and the Hiranya confluence, of Nagararka, Krishna, Sankarshana and the ocean,
the separate stories of Kumari, Kshetrapa and Brahmesha, of Pingalasangamesha, Shankararka and Ghatesha,
the account of Rishitirtha, Nandarka and Tritakupa, the wondrous stories of Sasopana, Parnarka and Nyankumati,
the account of Varahasvami, of Chhayalinga and Gulpha, the stories of Kanakananda, Kunti and Gangesha,
then the stories of Chamasodbheda, Vidura and Trilokesha, and likewise of Mankanesha, Traipuresha and Shandatirtha,
the stories of Suryaprachi, Trikshana and Umanata, of Bhudhara and Shulasthala, of Chyavanarka and Isha,
the stories of Ajapalesha, Balarka and Kuberasthala, the holy story of Rishitoya and the account of Sangaleshvara,
the account of Naradaditya, the exposition of Narayana, the greatness of Taptakunda and the description of Mulachandisha,
the story of the four-faced lord of the Ganas and of Kalambeshvara, the stories of Gopalasvami, Kulasvami and the Maruts,
then the stories of Kshemarka, Unnata-Vighnesha and Jalasvami, of Kalamegha, Rukmini, Durvaseshvara and Bhadra,
of Shankhavarta, Mokshatirtha, Goshpada and Achyuta's abode, the stories of Jaleshvara, Humkareshvara and Chandisha,
the wondrous story of Vighnesha at Ashapura and of Kalakunda, the story of Kapilesha and of Jaradgava-Shiva,
of Nala and Karkoteshvara, the story of Hatakeshvara, of Naradesha, Yantrabhusha, Durgakuta and Ganesha,
the stories of Suparna and the Bhairavi called Aila, of Bhallatirtha, the account of Kardamala and of Guptasomeshvara,
then the stories of Bahusvarnesha, Shringesha and Kotishvara, the grand story of Markandeshvara, Kotisha and Damodara's house,
Svarnarekha, Brahmakunda, Kunti and Bhimeshvara, and Mrigikunda — all this is remembered in the field of Vastrapatha;
the wondrous stories of Durga, Bhillesha, Gangesha and Raivata, then the story of Arbudeshvara and the account of Achaleshvara,
the story of Nagatirtha, the description of Vasishtha's hermitage, the greatness of Bhadrakarna and then of Trinetra,
the greatness of Kedara, the account of the arrival of the tirthas, then the stories of Kotishvara, Rupatirtha and Hrishikesha,
the account of Siddhesha, Shukreshvara and Manikarnisha, the description of Pangutirtha, Yamatirtha and Varahatirtha,
of Chandraprabhasa, Pindoda, Shrimata and Shuklatirtha, the greatness of Katyayani and then of Pindaraka,
then of Kanakhala, Chakratirtha and Manushatirtha, the story of Kapilagnitirtha and that of Raktanubandha,
of Ganesha and Partheshvara, of Yantra and Ujjvala, of Chandisthana, Nagodbhava, Shivakunda and Mahesha,
then the story of Kameshvara and the birth of Markandeya, the separate stories of Uddalakesha, Siddhesha and Gatatirtha,
the origin of Shridevaravata, of the tirthas of Vyasa and Gautama, the greatness of Kulasantara and the tirthas called Ramakoti,
the wondrous origin of Chandrodbheda, Ishanashringa and Brahmasthana, and the auspicious stories of Tripushkara, Rudrahrada and Guheshvara,
the greatness of Avimukta and of Umamaheshvara, the power of Mahaujas and the description of Jambutirtha,
the stories of Gangadhara and Mishraka and the praise of the fruit; in the greatness of Dvaraka the tale of Chandrasharma,
the account of vigils, worship and the like, the vow of Ekadashi, the story of the Mahadvadashi, the meeting of Prahlada and the sages,
the story of Durvasas, the account of the beginning of the pilgrimage, the story of the origin of the Gomati and the fruit of bathing and the like in it,
the greatness of Chakratirtha, the confluence of the Gomati and the ocean, the story of the lake of Sanaka and others, then the tale of Nrigatirtha,
the holy story of the grazing of cows, the coming of the gopis to Dvaraka, the story of Gopisaras and the account of Brahmatirtha and others,
the story of the arrival of the five rivers with many other stories, the account of Shivalinga, Gadatirtha, the worship of Krishna and the like,
the story of the image of Trivikrama, the conversation of Durvasas and Krishna, the slaying of the Daitya Kusha and the fruit of special worship,
the account of the arrival of the tirthas at the Gomati and Dvaraka, the viewing of Krishna's temple, the consecration of Dvaravati,
the story of the tirthas dwelling there and the account of the merit of Dvaraka — this is declared the seventh section, the Prabhasa, O brahmins.
In the Skanda, whose story surpasses all, in the description of Shiva's greatness — whoever writes this out and gives it with a golden trident
on the full moon of Magha, honouring a brahmin, rejoices in Shiva's abode.
The account of secondary creation — this is remembered as the Brahmi Samhita. After this, the exposition of the meaning of the Bhagavati Samhita,
where the separate livelihoods of the classes are declared: in its first part the conduct of brahmins is declared,
always of the nature of good conduct, child, increasing enjoyment and happiness; in the second the livelihood of kshatriyas is properly declared,
resorting to which one shakes off sin here and goes to heaven; in the third the fourfold livelihood of the vaishya class is told,
practising which properly one gains the highest goal; and in its fourth part the livelihood of shudras is declared,
by which Shri's lord, who increases men's good, is pleased; then in its fifth part the livelihood of the mixed classes is told,
practising which one attains an excellent future destiny. Thus this second Samhita consists of five parts, O sage.
The third here is the Sauri, prescribing men's duties, sixfold, teaching success in the six rites to those with desires.
The fourth, called Vaishnava, is declared to grant liberation, in four parts, for the twice-born, the very form of Brahman.
They are declared in order to have six, four, two and five thousand verses.
This Kurma Purana grants the fruit of the four aims, and gives the highest goal to men who read and hear it.
Whoever writes it out with devotion and gives it with a golden tortoise to a brahmin at the solstice goes to the supreme goal.
Thus the concluding part together with the latter has been told; the Brahmanda Purana in four parts has been declared to you,
the eighteenth, incomparable, the essence of essences, O brahmin. The Brahmanda Purana of four lakh verses by which it is recited —
that has been declared here separately in eighteen parts by the sage Parashara's son for all, O giver of honour.
In truth, having heard the Puranas from me, the teacher, the sages of cultivated minds made them known to the world —
those sages devoted to dharma, showing grace to the lowly. And this Purana was told by me long ago to Vasishtha;
he told it to Shakti's son, and he to Jatukarnya; Vyasa then received it as it came from the mouth of Prabhanjana,
and establishing it as authoritative, set this unsurpassed one going in the world. Whoever recites it, child, or hears it with concentration,
shakes off his sins here and goes to the world free from ill. Whoever writes out this Purana, placed on a golden lion-throne,
covered with cloth, and gives it to a brahmin goes to Brahma's world; there is no need to doubt this.
O Marichi, these eighteen Puranas that I have told you in brief should also be heard in full.
The best of men who hears the eighteen Puranas or recites them according to rule is not born here again.
This thread of the Puranas that I have now told you should be studied daily by one who desires the fruit of the Puranas.
It should never be given to the hypocrite, the sinner, one who envies gods and teachers, one who hates the good, or the deceitful;
it should be given to the peaceful, the calm-minded, one devoted to service, the unenvious, the pure and the true Vaishnava.
One who seeks enjoyment and liberation should read it for nine days; the worship of maidens there with food and the like is commended.
Having kept the vow thus, O brahmin, a man becomes an abode of all success on earth by Durga's grace; there is no doubt.
Then on the first day of the bright fortnight of Urja one should keep what is prescribed for the Navaratra, and especially the Annakuta, which increases Vishnu's pleasure.
With all kinds of cooked food, with all milk products, with everything, for the accomplishment of all aims, the Annakuta should be made in the worship of Govardhana.
In the evening, worshipping the glorious Govardhana, upholder of the earth, with the cows, and circumambulating it, one attains enjoyment and liberation.
Then on the first of the bright half of Margashirsha is the unsurpassed Dhana vow: worshipping Vishnu at night with oblations, a golden image of Fire
covered with a pair of red cloths should be given to a brahmin; having done so, one becomes rich in wealth and grain on earth,
and with sins burnt by fire, one is honoured in Vishnu's world. On the first of the bright half of Pausha, worshipping the Sun with devotion,
a mortal keeping the vow of one meal a day attains the Sun's world. On the first day of the bright half of Magha, worshipping Fire, who is Maheshvara himself,
duly, one becomes prosperous on earth. Then at the beginning of the bright half of Phalguna, the naked God of gods,
all his limbs grey with dust, one should sprinkle all over with water; for Maheshvara is pleased even with a worldly act,
and, worshipped rightly with devotion, grants union with himself. On the first of the bright half of Vaishakha, worshipping Vishnu, who sports in the universe,
duly, the vow-keeper should feed brahmins; likewise on the first of the bright half of Shuchi, Brahma, teacher of the worlds;
Brahma, together with Vishnu, lord of the lords of all worlds, grants union with himself, and one attains all success.
These vows on the first days of the twelve months, O best of brahmins, I have told you; they grant enjoyment and liberation.
In all these vows celibacy is prescribed, and in eating, sacrificial food is generally declared.
The gift of the half-moon is declared here, granting all success. On the second of the bright half of Bhadra, worshipping the ordainer of the world in the form of Shakra
duly, one gains the fruit of all sacrifices. In the month of Ashvina the second day of the bright half is holy;
a gift given on it is said to have endless fruit. On the second of the bright half of Urja, long ago, Yama was fed by Yamuna
in her own house; so this second day is called Yama's. Eating at one's sister's house on this day increases nourishment,
and after that one should give her clothes and ornaments.
On the day when the god Yamaraja was fed by Yamuna with her own hand out of sisterly love, whoever eats from his sister's hand obtains unsurpassed gems, wealth and grain.
On the second of the bright half of Margashirsha one should worship the ancestors with shraddha; one gains health and continuity of sons and grandsons.
On the second of the bright half of Pausha, sprinkling with water from a cow's horn and seeing the new moon grant men all desires.
Whoever, eating sacrificial food and with senses controlled, worships the new moon with an arghya and flowers with ghee gains dharma, pleasure and wealth.
On the second of the bright half of Magha one should duly worship Prajapati in the form of the Sun with red flowers
and red perfumes, and, making a golden image according to one's means, then offering to the god with devotion a copper vessel full of wheat or rice,
give the image to a brahmin. When this vow is kept, O brahmin, a man becomes like the risen sun himself,
unapproachable and invincible on earth; enjoying excellent desires here, at the end he goes to Brahma's state,
constantly praised by all the gods, seated in an excellent celestial car. Then on the second of the bright half of Phalguna, the best of brahmins,
worshipping Shiva with very white, fragrant flowers, making a canopy of flowers with fine flower ornaments,
pleasing him with various food offerings, incense, lamps and waving of lights, should prostrate himself fully on the ground.
Worshipping the Lord of gods thus, a mortal, free from disease and endowed with wealth and grain, surely lives a hundred years.
The procedure declared for the second days of the bright fortnights should be followed by those who know the rules on those of the dark fortnights too.
Fire alone, bearing various bodily forms in the different months, is worshipped on the second days, with celibacy and the rest as before.
The woman who keeps this vow that increases good fortune surely gains good fortune by the Goddess's grace.
When the third day in Bhadra falls with the constellation Hasta, that is declared by Shauri to be the Hastagauri vow;
likewise the vow called Kotishvari is declared by the Pinaka-bearer, and Lakshasvari too; its procedure is now told.
This vow should be taken up for four years, kept with a fast year after year, O Narada.
Cleaning a lakh of unbroken rice grains or sesame, O lord of sages, one should put them into boiling milk,
and with that cooked mass make a very beautiful image of the Goddess, adorned with a heap of perfumes and flowers and with flower garlands;
installing Parvati there, one should worship her, filled with devotion, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps and abundant food offerings,
and various fruits, O brahmin, bow and ask forgiveness; then one should immerse the Goddess in water,
give fees to brahmins who know the rules, and eat on the next day. Thus the Kotilakshesvari vow has been told to you, O brahmin;
by its power one goes to Gauri's world at the end. On the third of the bright half of Isha one should keep the Brihadgauri vow
for five years by the procedure described before, O Narada; at the end one should honour the teacher and other brahmins with wealth and the like,
and five married women should be honoured with clothes, ornaments and sandal, with bodices, earrings and neck-threads, O beloved of Hari;
five bamboo vessels wrapped with threads, with vermilion, cumin and articles of good fortune,
with wheat-flour preparations, fresh cakes, fruits and the like — five such gifts one should give them and feed them.
Having given the arghya and the gifts, one should eat afterwards in silence, and wear that fruit on the neck for the fulfilment of all desires.
Then, rising in the morning, adorned, with her women friends, with songs and music, she should immerse that Gauri in the river:
O auspicious one, you were invoked and worshipped by me duly; to grant me good fortune, go as you wish.
Having kept the vow thus with devotion, O brahmin, by the Goddess's grace one enjoys pleasures and at the body's end attains Gauri's world.
On the third of the bright half of Urja one should keep the Vishnugauri vow, worshipping the one revered by the world with various offerings,
and feeding a married woman honoured with auspicious articles, bowing to her, one should dismiss her, for the pleasure of Vishnugauri.
On the third of the bright half of Margashirsha, keeping the auspicious Haragauri vow by the earlier procedure, one should worship the Mother of the world;
by the power of this vow, enjoying delightful pleasures, one reaches the Goddess's world and rejoices with her.
On the third of the bright half of Pausha one should keep the Brahmagauri vow; worshipped by the earlier procedure, O best of brahmins,
by Brahmagauri's grace one rejoices there in her company. On the third of the bright half of Magha, Saubhagyasundari is to be worshipped
by the earlier procedure, with the gift of a coconut as arghya; pleased by the vow, she grants her own world.
In the bright half of Phalguna, the third day brings happiness to the family; worshipped with perfumes, flowers and the like, she grants all blessings.
On all third days the general procedure, O sage, is the worship of the Goddess, worship of brahmins, gifts, oblation and immersion.
Thus the vows of the third day have been told to you here; performed with devotion, they grant the desires in the mind.
honoured by the hosts of gods, one attains Goloka. Then on the fourth of the bright half is the vow of Siddhivinayaka:
worship with all the offerings beginning with invocation; with a one-pointed mind one should meditate on Siddhivinayaka,
single-tusked, with winnowing-basket ears, elephant-faced, four-armed, holding noose and goad, like molten gold.
With devotion one should offer twenty-one leaves with twenty-one names; hear those names:
a shami leaf to Sumukha, a bhringa leaf to Ganadhisha, a bilva leaf to Umaputra, durva to Gajamukha,
a jujube leaf to Lambodara, datura to Harasunu, tulasi to Shurpakarna, a bean leaf to Vakratunda,
apamarga to Guhagraja, brihati to Ekadanta, sindura to Heramba, and a patra leaf to Chaturhotri,
and to Sarveshvara an agastya leaf, which increases his pleasure. Then taking a pair of durva blades with perfume, flowers and unbroken rice,
one should offer the worship with devotion and five modakas; offering water for sipping, bowing and praying, one should dismiss him.
A golden image of Vinayaka with its accessories, O sage, should be given to the teacher, and fees to brahmins.
Worshipping thus with devotion for five years, O Narada, one gains auspicious desires of this world and the next.
On this fourth day one should never look at the moon; if one looks, one surely incurs false accusation. To remove that fault one should recite the Puranic mantra:
A lion killed Prasena, and the lion was slain by Jambavan; do not weep, little boy, this Syamantaka is yours.
On the fourth of the bright half of Isha, Vinayaka the lord of cowries
should be worshipped with the Purusha hymn and offerings; rice grains taken in a fistful without counting, with cowries,
should be given to a brahmin boy worshipped with perfumes and flowers; the rice grains belong to the Vishvedevas, mixed with those belonging to Hara:
May that Kapardi, lord of the Ganas, be pleased with these offerings. On the fourth of the dark half of Kartika the vow called Karaka is remembered;
only women are entitled to it; its procedure is told. Having bathed and adorned herself, the woman should worship the lord of the Ganas,
and before him place ten pitchers of fully cooked food, offering them to the God of gods with devotion and a restrained mind,
saying, "May the god be pleased with me," and then give them respectfully to married women and brahmins as they wish.
Then at night, at moonrise, having given the arghya duly, she should eat sweet food to complete the vow.
Or, O sage, a pitcher full of milk or water, with betel nut, unbroken rice and gems, should be given to a brahmin.
Having kept this vow for sixteen or twelve years, a woman should make the concluding gifts and then conclude the vow,
or a woman may keep it all her life out of desire for good fortune; there is nothing like this vow for giving women good fortune
in all the worlds; therefore it is established as perpetual. On the fourth of the bright half of Urja the Naga vow is declared.
Making the vow's resolve in the morning, drinking pure water from a cow's horn and bathing, at midday one should invoke the serpents beginning with Shankhapala,
and Shesha, and worship them with offerings, and refresh them with milk — this is remembered as the Naga vow.
